## 4. Game of Craps
The code below defines a couple of functions to simulate a game of craps, 
as defined by the exercise sheet.
The main idea to simulate a game of craps is simple:

1. Execute a function to generate dice rolls.
2. Depending on the previous output, decide outcome of the round.

The first step then is to figure out how to generate a roll dice in R.
After some research, the function `sample()`, has been found. Having a quick
look at `?sample()` we can go and implement the following function:

```{r}
roll_die <- function() {
  return(sample(1:6, 1, replace = TRUE))
}
```

We specifically overwrite the default parameter `replace` to be `TRUE`, which
is equal to say that consecutive dice rolls are independent from one another.
With this in hand, the remaining code is straight forward.

```{r}
# Simulate a single round of game of craps
play_craps <- function() {
  point_number <- roll_die() # First roll
  print(paste("First roll was:", point_number))

  if (point_number == 6) {
    print("Congrats, you won!")
    return(TRUE) # Inmediate win
  } else if (point_number == 1) {
    print("Oops, you lost...")
    return(FALSE) # Inmediate loss
  }

  # Roll up to three more times to match point number
  for (i in 1:3) {
    roll <- roll_die()
    print(paste("Roll", i, "is:", roll))
    if (roll == point_number) {
      print("Congrats, you won!")
      return(TRUE) # Player wins
    }
  }
  # After three rolls, round is lost
  print("Bad luck, maybe next time :)")
  return(FALSE)
}
```
Let us play a couple of rounds...
```{r}
play_craps()
play_craps()
play_craps()
```



## 5. Readable and efficient code
```R
set.seed(1)
x <- rnorm(1000)
y <- 2 + x + rnorm(1000)
df <- data.frame(x, y)

cat("Step", 1, "\n")
fit1 <- lm(y ~ x, data = df[-(1:250),])
p1 <- predict(fit1, newdata = df[(1:250),])
r <- sqrt(mean((p1 - df[(1:250),"y"])^2))

cat("Step", 2, "\n")
fit2 <- lm(y ~ x, data = df[-(251:500),])
p2 <- predict(fit2, newdata = df[(251:500),])
r <- c(r, sqrt(mean((p2 - df[(251:500),"y"])^2)))

cat("Step", 3, "\n")
fit3 <- lm(y ~ x, data = df[-(501:750),])
p3 <- predict(fit3, newdata = df[(501:750),])
r <- c(r, sqrt(mean((p3 - df[(501:750),"y"])^2)))

cat("Step", 4, "\n")
fit4 <- lm(y ~ x, data = df[-(751:1000),])
p4 <- predict(fit4, newdata = df[(751:1000),])
r <- c(r, sqrt(mean((p4 - df[(751:1000),"y"])^2)))
r
```
#### a. Code explanation
This code executes four times a linear regression on the same set of data, 
modifing each time just the subset of data used to train and test the model. 
For every model, the RMSE (root mean squared error) is computed 
on the test subset. The result is appended to a vector, which is finally 
*returned*.


#### b. Changes to improve readability
Several measures can be employed to improve the readability of the code. The 
first one is renaming variables. Although `p1` might be easy to write, does very 
little in terms of helping to undertand what the variable represents. Same goes 
for the variable `r`.

Another potential improvement is to set a new variable to indicate the interval 
in which train/test data will be split. This yields not only more readable code, 
but also easy access to modify the interval with just one variable.

The final and most important improvement in readability is to actually use the
RMSE function provided by the `Metrics` package in R, instead of writting the 
long `sqrt(mean(...))`.

#### c. Function wrapping
<!-- Function should have at most 10 lines... it has 12 -->
```{r}
library("Metrics")

linear_model_rsme <- function(formula, data, partitions = 4) {
  if (partitions < nrow(data) && partitions > 2) {
    result <- vector("numeric", length = partitions)

    for (i in seq(0, partitions - 1)) {
      interval <- ((i * nrow(data) / partitions) + 1):
        ((i + 1) * nrow(data) / partitions)
      model <- lm(formula, data[-(interval), ])
      predictions <- predict(model, newdata = data[interval, ])
      result[i + 1] <- rmse(data[interval, "y"], predictions)
    }
    return(result)
  } else {
    return(c(NA))
  }
}
```
*Please note: if `x <- 1; y <- 2` counts as two lines, we have taken the liberty*
*to say that:*
```R
interval <- (1 + i * nrow(data) / partitions):
            ((i + 1) * nrow(data) / partitions)
```
*counts as only one*.

**Performing checks**


```{r}
r <- linear_model_rsme(y ~ x, df)
r
```
